newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF, Bulgaria aim for prudent 1997 budget deficit.
newsitem.headline: IMF, Bulgaria aim for prudent 1997 budget deficit.

text.p: Bulgaria must aim for a prudent 1997 budget deficit in order to sustain a strict fixed exchange rate regime to stabilise the economy, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Wednesday.
"The budget is the bottom line. We are trying to agree on a fiscal deficit that we think is prudent," IMF team leader Anne McGuirk told Reuters.
The IMF mission arrived in Sofia two weeks ago to help prepare the introduction of a currency board.
This is a self-regulating mechanism where the lev is pegged to an anchor currency and the amount of levs in circulation must be fully covered by the foreign exchange reserves.
The system bans the central bank from lending to commercial banks and government.

A $657 million reform and funding deal with the IMF envisages trimming the budget deficit in 1997 to 3.8 percent of GDP from 10.9 percent last year by eliminating the need for central bank credit to the government and through spending cuts.
This year's budget is assumed at a lev/dollar exchange rate of 1,600 or 1,000 levs to the mark, said Finance Minister Muravei Radev on Tuesday.

"I think that we have cleared all issues on structural reform, the main remaining task is to work on the budget and a few issues in the banking system," said McGuirk, whose mission is due to end on Friday.
"There are just some final things. We have to agree on the technical assistance programme for banking supervision," she added.
Under the agreement Bulgaria needs to strengthen bank supervision and, where neccessary, upgrade its banking regulations to accord with international standards.
Under the deal the government is also expected to increase capital adequacy requirements to six percent by end-1997 and 10 percent by end-1998.
McGuirk said they hoped to complete the work on the budget by Friday. The budget then needs to pass through cabinet and parliamentary approval.
The anchor currency and rate at which it will be fixed will be decided by parliament and announced few days before the currency board system is introduced.
The new reformist government, which took office last week, said the system will be introduced on July 1 and proposed the mark to be its anchor.

The IMF will consider disbursing a second tranche of the standby arrangement after the currency board system is in place and Bulgaria has met the reform targets for the first review, said McGuirk. --Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-981-4145
